title: How to create a client portal in 5 simple steps
summary: Learn how to create a client portal in five clear steps, from planning to launch, and give clients an organized way to track projects.
body_markdown:
Picture this: a client emails you for the third time this week asking where their contract stands, whether you got their last payment, and what the project timeline looks like. If you're juggling that kind of back-and-forth across email, spreadsheets, and text messages, you already know the cost of not having a central hub. Learning how to create a client portal is one of the more practical fixes available, since it gives clients a single, secure place to check proposals, invoices, and project progress without pinging you directly. Before you settle on a platform, it helps to start by comparing CRM (customer relationship management) tools worth considering, since many portals live inside a broader client management system rather than as a standalone product. This guide walks through five concrete steps to create a client portal, from scoping requirements to launching it with real clients, so you can build something clients actually use instead of another tool that gathers dust.

## What is a client portal, and why does your business need one?


A client portal is a secure, branded space where clients log in to view project updates, files, invoices, and proposals, without sending you another email. Instead of digging through old threads to find a contract or attachment, clients get one link that shows exactly where things stand. That single-hub approach can help address the scattered communication problem: lost attachments, duplicate status update requests, and details buried across email, spreadsheets, and text messages.


This matters most for freelancers and small agencies managing several active clients at once, where repeating the same updates eats into billable time. If you're still relying on manual habits to stay organized, it's worth reading how to keep track of clients effectively before you build out a portal, since the two practices reinforce each other.


## Step 1: define what your client portal needs to do


Before you compare tools, get specific about what your clients actually need to see and do. A portal built around a generic feature list often ends up half-used, while one scoped to real client questions tends to stick. Start by listing the tasks that currently create back-and-forth: approving a proposal, checking an invoice, downloading a file, or confirming a milestone.


### Core features clients expect


Most clients expect a baseline of file access, invoice visibility, and project status at a glance. Beyond that, prioritize two or three must-haves rather than trying to pack in as many features as possible. A crowded portal with options clients rarely use adds setup work without solving the original problem.


- **File sharing:** contracts, deliverables, and reference documents stored together for easy access
- **Invoice viewing:** current balance and payment history
- **Proposal tracking:** status of pending approvals
- **Project status:** milestones or progress at a glance
- **Messaging:** a lightweight way to ask questions without email


### Match features to your service type


A freelance designer might prioritize file sharing and proposal approval, while a consultant leans on project status and invoice visibility. Agencies with recurring retainers often need messaging and progress tracking most, since clients check in between billing cycles rather than at project milestones.


## Step 2: choose the right platform for your client portal


Once you know what the portal needs to do, the next decision is where it should live. Some tools focus narrowly on sharing files and status updates, while others fold the portal into a broader system that also handles client records, invoicing, and contracts.


### Standalone portal builders vs. bundled CRM platforms


A standalone portal builder can work fine if your main need is a simple space for file sharing and updates. The trade-off is that client details, invoices, and signed contracts still live somewhere else, so you're back to checking multiple tools. A bundled[Bonsai CRM](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/crm/) and portal setup keeps that information connected to the same client record instead of scattered across separate logins.


### What to budget for a client portal


Costs typically scale with per-user pricing, add-on features, and how many active clients you're managing at once. Before committing, it helps to spend time understanding CRM pricing so you know what's reasonable for your client roster and which add-ons are worth paying for versus skipping.

## Step 3: set up your portal structure and branding


Once you've picked a platform, the way you organize the portal determines whether clients find things quickly or give up and email you anyway. Structure and branding are quick to set up, but skipping them creates confusion later as your client list grows.


### Organize your portal by client or project


Most freelancers find it effective to organize by client, with each client record holding their proposals, invoices, and files in one spot. Agencies running multiple concurrent projects per client may prefer a project-based structure instead, especially when a single client has separate contracts running at once. Pick one approach early since restructuring later means re-sorting files for each active client.


### Add your branding


A portal that shows your logo, brand colors, and a custom domain or subdomain (where supported) reads as a professional extension of your business rather than a generic third-party tool. Keep navigation to one or two clicks so clients can find an invoice or file without searching.


## Step 4: add security and access permissions


A client portal only works if each client sees their own information and nothing else. Getting permissions right can help protect client confidentiality and reduce the risk of accidentally exposing one client's invoice or contract to another.


### Set access permissions per client


Each client should only see their own proposals, invoices, and files, not a shared view that spans your whole client list. Setting this up per client, rather than relying on one broad login for everyone, keeps records separated as your roster grows. This matters most for agencies managing several active projects at once, where a mix-up between client records creates real trust problems.


### Protect sensitive documents


Look for a platform where clients access the portal through a secure magic link instead of a shared password, since that removes one more credential for clients to lose or reuse elsewhere. Documents should also be stored in the cloud with encryption at rest, so contracts and financial files stay protected whether they're actively in use or sitting archived. Confirming both of these before launch is a reasonable baseline check, not an advanced setup step.


## Step 5: launch and onboard your clients


With structure, branding, and permissions in place, the last step is rolling the portal out to clients without overwhelming them. A rushed launch, where many clients get an invite on the same day, tends to generate a flood of login questions at once. Start with one or two clients, work out any rough edges, then extend the portal to the rest of your roster over the following weeks.


### Send a clear onboarding message


The first email or magic-link invite should explain how to log in, what they'll find inside, and who to contact with questions. Keep it short: a line on accessing the portal, a note on what's already loaded (proposals, invoices, files), and a reminder that no password setup is required.


### Migrate existing client data


Before inviting anyone, move historical files, signed contracts, and past invoices into the new portal so clients see a complete record rather than a blank slate. This step often takes longer than expected, so it's worth following a guide to CRM migration for freelancers and small businesses to avoid losing records in the switch.


## How Bonsai helps with creating a client portal


Most of the setup work described above (organizing by client, applying branding, and separating access) is built into Bonsai's client portal rather than something you configure from scratch. Clients access the portal through a secure magic link, so there's no shared password to manage or reset when a client forgets their login. The portal is also branded, with three modes to choose from: Bonsai branding, your own branding, or no branding, so a design freelancer can hand a client a portal that looks like an extension of their own studio rather than a third-party tool.


Because the portal sits on top of[Bonsai CRM](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/crm/) , each client's records, notes, and communication history live in the same place the portal pulls from. A consultant running four retainer clients at $2,000 a month doesn't need to rebuild the portal structure per client: the CRM record already holds the project history, and the portal simply surfaces the pieces each client is allowed to see.


The portal also connects directly to the documents clients ask about most. When a proposal goes out through[Bonsai proposals](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/proposals/) , the client can review and approve it from inside their portal, and an accepted proposal generates the matching invoice without anyone re-entering line items. That invoice then shows up through[Bonsai invoicing](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/invoicing/) , so a client checking on a $3,200 project balance sees current status without emailing to ask. Because Bonsai integrates with Zoom, meeting transcripts from client calls can sync to the same client record, so a decision made on a Zoom call is logged alongside the proposal and invoice history instead of getting lost in a separate app. For a freelancer or small agency juggling several active clients, that combination is designed to help cut down on the number of scattered logins clients need to check, since proposals, invoices, and project status live in the same connected client record.


## FAQ


### **Q1: What is a client portal?**


A client portal is a secure, branded space where clients log in to view proposals, invoices, files, and project updates without emailing you directly. Instead of digging through scattered threads, clients get a single link that shows exactly where things stand on their project or account. Most portals also support messaging, so clients can ask a quick question without starting a new email chain.


Portals are most useful for freelancers and small agencies managing multiple active clients at once, where repeating the same status updates eats into billable time. Rather than existing as a standalone product, a client portal typically lives inside a broader CRM or client management system, which keeps the information it displays connected to the same client record.


### **Q2: How do I create my own client portal?**


Creating a client portal starts with defining what your clients actually need to see, such as invoices, files, proposal status, or project progress, rather than picking a tool first. From there, choose a platform, organize it by client or project, apply your branding, and set access permissions so each client sees only their own information.


The last step is launching with a small group of clients before rolling it out to your full roster, and migrating historical files and invoices so the portal shows a complete record from day one. Working through these steps in order, requirements first and tool choice second, tends to produce a portal clients actually use instead of one that sits unopened.


### **Q3: How do you create a customer portal for your business?**


Creating a customer portal follows largely the same process as a client portal: scope what customers need to check on their own (orders, invoices, project status, files), then choose a platform that supports those features without unnecessary extras. Structure the portal by customer or account, add your branding so it feels like part of your business rather than a generic third-party tool, and set permissions so each customer's data stays separate.


Businesses that serve a high volume of customers often prioritize invoice visibility and file access first, since those generate the most repetitive support requests. Testing the portal with a handful of customers before a full rollout helps catch confusing navigation or missing information early.


### **Q4: How do I create a portal for my business without hiring a developer?**


Most small businesses build a client portal using an existing CRM or portal platform rather than custom development, since these tools handle the login system, permissions, and branding out of the box. You typically configure the portal through a dashboard: uploading your logo, organizing client records, and toggling what each client can see, without writing code.


This approach is usually faster and more budget-friendly than a custom build, and it comes with security and access controls already built in rather than something you'd need to engineer yourself. For most freelancers and agencies, a no-code platform covers the core needs (files, invoices, proposals, and messaging) without the ongoing maintenance a custom-built portal would require.


### **Q5: Is it expensive to create a client portal?**


Cost depends heavily on the platform, since pricing typically scales with per-user fees, add-on features, and the number of active clients you're managing. A standalone portal builder with limited features may cost less upfront, but bundling the portal into a broader CRM platform can reduce the need for separate tools to manage invoices and contracts.


Before committing to a plan, it's worth comparing what different providers include at each pricing tier, since features and costs vary and change over time. Reviewing current pricing directly on a provider's pricing page is a more reliable check than relying on older comparisons.


### **Q6: How does Bonsai help with creating a client portal?**


Bonsai's client portal is built into its CRM, so client records, branding, and access permissions come largely pre-configured rather than requiring setup from scratch. Clients access the portal through a secure magic link, removing the need for a shared password, and the portal supports three branding modes: Bonsai branding, your own branding, or no branding.


Because the portal connects to the same client record used across proposals, invoices, and communication history, a client checking their portal sees current, accurate status rather than outdated information. Meeting transcripts from Zoom calls can also sync to that client record, so decisions made during a call are logged alongside the rest of the client's history.


Creating a client portal comes down to scoping what clients actually need, choosing a platform that fits your budget, and setting up structure, branding, and permissions before you launch. Skipping straight to a tool without that groundwork is usually why a portal ends up half-used. Whether you build it as a standalone tool or as part of a bundled CRM like Bonsai, the goal stays the same: help clients spend less time juggling separate inboxes by keeping proposals, invoices, and project updates connected to one client record.
